Tense and aspect receive meanings at the opening. Modal verb, ability, permission, obligation, and possibility receive definitions or plain examples before their worked applications. No prerequisite teaching is assumed for the named patterns.
Time/aspect teaching gives formation and choice cues for all six forms. Present perfect explains present result, life experience, continuing state, and repeated events up to now.

Voice teaching explains subject/receiver roles, preserves time in conversions, and distinguishes be/get states from passives. Modal teaching explains present/past ability, degrees of permission politeness, requirement/advice/ban/optionality, overlapping possibility, and inferential must.

Checked the stated limits: state verbs usually take simple forms; finished past times normally take simple past; before can make past perfect optional; usual passive conversion needs an object; get-passives suit informal contexts and be-passives formal reports.

Modal limitations include could for general past ability, permission register differences, must not versus do not have to, possibility overlap, and the evidence-based non-obligation use of must. These conditions guide the examples and shortcuts.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Choose the correct form: I think the office *(will close / closed)* early tomorrow.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: Examples 3 through 6 now exercise future will, present progressive, and the present-perfect uses alongside simple past and past perfect.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Tense helps show when something happens.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The abstract original sentence is split into short explanations of tense and aspect with concrete uses later.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Rewrite the sentence with the correct verb forms: "Yesterday, she walks to the store and bought bread."
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The former bare sentence now has a clear correction task. This fixes that specific brief item despite the separate Example 7 issue.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: A **past participle** is a verb form used after *has, have,* or *had* and in many passive forms.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The term is explained before passive formation, with regular and irregular participle examples.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: This form can show a present result: "She has finished the report, so it is ready now."
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The passage also explains experience, continuing situations, and repeated events in an unfinished period. Examples 5 and 6 apply these meanings.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Complete the sentence using the past perfect form of *finish*: "By the time the meeting started, Ana ___ the report."
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The explicit past-perfect requirement makes had finished unique. Supplying that requirement creates the separate L05 finding recorded above.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: **Future meaning with will** uses *will + base form*.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Core Concept gives prediction, promise, future statement, and immediate-decision uses. Example 3 selects will close and explains the prediction cue.
Formation and subject agreement are explicit. Examples 5 and 6 choose the form using links to now and contrast a finished past time.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: A **get-passive** uses *get + past participle*: "The package got delivered."
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Core Concept explains informal use and formal be-passive preference. Example 10 identifies an action received and converts the sentence for a formal report.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: For **ability**, use *can* for present or general ability.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Can and could are contrasted for present and general past ability. Example 11 applies both choices with time cues.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: For **permission**, *can* is common in everyday requests.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: The passage contrasts everyday can, formal may, and polite could. Example 12 selects may for formal permission.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: For **obligation**, *must* and *have to* show a strong requirement.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Requirement, advice, prohibition, and lack of requirement are distinguished. Examples 13 and 14 apply the contrasts.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: For **possibility**, *may, might,* and *could* can all mean that something is possible: "It might rain later."
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: The overlap is explicit, avoiding an unsupported unique ranking. Example 15 selects possibility against a requirement reading.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Which sentence uses a get-passive: "The package got delivered before noon" or "The package got heavy in the rain"?
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: Example 10 now works the get-passive/state distinction. Example 8 also contrasts a be-passive with be plus a description.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: 1. *Yesterday* places both actions in past time.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The correction solution now uses a numbered list with the time cue, changed verb, and complete corrected sentence.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Use it for a prediction, promise, future statement, or decision made as you speak: "I will help you."
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: Will now has explicit selection conditions and a formation rule. Example 3 applies the prediction use.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: It is common in speech and informal writing; use a *be*-passive when a formal style is needed.
